topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under Georgia's Restrictive Covenants Act, O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53, is a post-employment non-compete covenant generally enforceable against a rank-and-file employee who does not fall into a specific exempted category?
choice_a: No -- post-employment non-competes are generally unenforceable except against employees who fall into specific categories, such as those who regularly solicit customers, regularly make sales, hold qualifying management authority, or qualify as key employees or professionals
choice_b: Yes -- Georgia enforces a post-employment non-compete against any employee regardless of role or job duties
choice_c: No -- Georgia categorically bans all non-compete covenants for every category of worker with no exceptions
choice_d: Yes, but only if the employee earns above the state's median household income
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53 generally makes post-employment non-competes unenforceable against most employees, but permits them against employees who regularly solicit customers or prospective customers, regularly make sales or obtain contracts for the employer's services, hold qualifying management authority, or qualify as key employees or professionals -- categories that commonly capture licensed real estate salespeople and associate brokers.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53, what general standard must a non-compete covenant satisfy to be enforceable, even against an employee in one of the qualifying categories?
choice_a: It need only be reasonable in scope, with no limitation whatsoever on time or geographic area
choice_b: It must be reasonable in time, geographic area, and scope of the prohibited activities
choice_c: It must last for the employee's entire lifetime to be considered valid
choice_d: It need not be in writing to be enforceable under Georgia law
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53 requires an enforceable non-compete covenant to be reasonable in time, geographic area, and scope of the prohibited activities -- an unreasonably broad restriction in any of these dimensions risks being unenforceable.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53, what standard does a written non-solicitation-of-customers covenant use to define which customers the departing employee may not solicit?
choice_a: The restriction automatically applies to every customer the employer has ever served, regardless of the departing employee's own contact with them
choice_b: Non-solicitation covenants have no permissible standard and are entirely unenforceable in Georgia
choice_c: The 'material contact' standard -- the restriction applies only to customers the employee actually had material contact with during employment, for a stated period following termination
choice_d: The restriction may only apply to customers acquired during the departing employee's first year of employment
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53 permits a written non-solicitation covenant limited to customers the departing employee had 'material contact' with during employment, running for a stated period after termination -- a narrower, more targeted standard than a blanket restriction covering the entire employer customer base.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53, if a court finds a restrictive covenant overbroad, what 'blue pencil' authority does the statute give the court regarding modification?
choice_a: The court has no authority to modify an overbroad covenant and must strike it down entirely with no alternative
choice_b: The court may freely rewrite the covenant to be broader than originally drafted if doing so better protects the employer
choice_c: Only the employee, never a court, has the authority to modify an overbroad covenant
choice_d: The court may modify (narrow) an overbroad covenant to make it reasonable, but may not make it MORE restrictive than the parties originally drafted
explanation: O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53 gives Georgia courts 'blue pencil' authority to modify an overly broad restrictive covenant to bring it within reasonable bounds, but the statute does not allow the court to rewrite the covenant to be more restrictive than the parties' original agreement.

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: A qualifying broker asks a newly affiliated associate broker to sign a written agreement restricting the associate broker, for one year after leaving the firm, from soliciting only those specific clients the associate broker personally worked with while affiliated. Is a covenant drafted this way consistent with O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53's requirements for a non-solicitation covenant?
choice_a: Yes -- limiting the restriction to a stated time period and to customers the departing licensee had material contact with is consistent with the statute's framework for an enforceable non-solicitation covenant
choice_b: No -- any non-solicitation covenant of any kind is automatically void in Georgia regardless of how narrowly it is drafted
choice_c: No -- the covenant must cover every client the firm has ever served, not just those the departing licensee personally worked with, to be valid
choice_d: Yes, but only if the covenant also includes a lifetime restriction with no stated end date
explanation: A non-solicitation covenant limited to a stated time period and to customers the departing licensee had material contact with tracks O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53's framework for an enforceable covenant, in contrast to an unlimited-duration restriction or one sweeping in every customer the firm has ever served.
source_note: O.C.G.A. § 13-8-53 (applied to a broker-associate-broker restrictive covenant scenario)

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: Under RESPA, does an 'affiliated business arrangement' (AfBA) -- such as a real estate brokerage that also owns an interest in a title company or mortgage company it refers clients to -- automatically violate RESPA's anti-kickback prohibition?
choice_a: Yes -- any affiliated business arrangement is automatically and categorically illegal under RESPA with no exceptions
choice_b: No -- RESPA provides a disclosure-based exemption for a properly structured and disclosed AfBA, so long as the referring party discloses the affiliated relationship in writing, the client is not required to use the affiliated provider, and no fee is exchanged for the referral itself beyond a permissible return on ownership investment
choice_c: No -- RESPA has no application whatsoever to affiliated business arrangements of any kind
choice_d: Yes, but only if the affiliated business is a title company specifically; affiliated mortgage companies are exempt from this rule
explanation: RESPA provides a specific exemption for a properly structured and disclosed affiliated business arrangement: the referring party must give the client a required written disclosure of the relationship, the client must not be required to use the affiliated provider, and no fee may be exchanged for the referral itself beyond a permissible return on the referring party's ownership interest -- an AfBA that fails these conditions can still violate RESPA's anti-kickback provisions.
source_note: hedge: standard federal RESPA affiliated-business-arrangement content

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a matter of general national law (federal E-SIGN Act and the widely adopted state Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, or UETA), does an electronic signature on a real estate contract generally have the same legal effect as a handwritten (wet-ink) signature?
choice_a: No -- an electronic signature has no legal validity for any real estate contract in any U.S. state
choice_b: Yes, but only for a purchase contract, never for a deed or other recorded instrument, in every U.S. jurisdiction without exception
choice_c: Yes, generally -- both the federal E-SIGN Act and state UETA-type statutes generally give electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as their handwritten/paper counterparts, provided the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction electronically and other statutory requirements are met
choice_d: No -- electronic signatures require a separate notarized paper ratification within 24 hours to be valid anywhere
explanation: The federal E-SIGN Act and state UETA-type statutes generally provide that electronic signatures and records carry the same legal effect as handwritten signatures and paper records for most transactions -- including real estate contracts -- provided the parties have agreed to transact electronically and the statute's other requirements are satisfied, though specific recording/notarization mechanics for certain instruments can involve additional considerations.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- federal E-SIGN Act and state UETA-type electronic-signature law

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a general matter of business-entity law, what is the purpose of designating a 'registered agent' for a corporation or LLC operating a real estate brokerage?
choice_a: A registered agent is simply another term for the firm's qualifying broker, with no separate corporate-law significance
choice_b: A registered agent is required only for entities with no employees
choice_c: A registered agent's sole function is to prepare the entity's annual tax return
choice_d: A registered agent is a designated person or entity authorized to receive legal notices, service of process, and official state correspondence on the business entity's behalf at a listed address
explanation: As a matter of general business-entity law, a registered agent is a person or entity designated to receive legal notices, service of process, and official state correspondence on behalf of a corporation or LLC at a listed address -- a corporate-law formality distinct from the real-estate-specific role of a firm's qualifying broker.
source_note: hedge: standard national business-entity-law content, not Georgia-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a matter of general national practice, how does the NAR (National Association of REALTORS®) Code of Ethics relate to a state's real estate license law, such as Georgia's?
choice_a: The NAR Code of Ethics is a private, membership-based ethical standard that applies only to licensees who choose to become NAR members ('REALTORS®'), imposing obligations in addition to (and sometimes exceeding) the minimum conduct standards set by state license law -- state license law itself applies to every licensee regardless of NAR membership
choice_b: The NAR Code of Ethics is simply another name for state license law and imposes no separate obligations
choice_c: Only unlicensed real estate assistants are subject to the NAR Code of Ethics
choice_d: A GREC-licensed real estate professional is automatically bound by the NAR Code of Ethics whether or not they join a REALTOR® association
explanation: The NAR Code of Ethics is a private, voluntary-membership standard binding only on licensees who join a REALTOR® association ('REALTORS®'), imposing additional (and sometimes stricter) ethical obligations beyond the baseline conduct standards state license law imposes on every licensee, member or not.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- NAR Code of Ethics versus state license law, not Georgia-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a matter of general national franchise-law doctrine, what does it typically mean for an independently owned real estate brokerage to operate under a national franchise brand?
choice_a: The franchisor becomes the licensed qualifying broker of every franchised location automatically
choice_b: The local brokerage remains an independently owned and operated business (with its own licensure, liabilities, and management) that has contracted with a franchisor for the right to use the franchisor's brand, systems, and marketing in exchange for fees, typically under terms disclosed in a franchise disclosure document
choice_c: Franchising eliminates the need for the local brokerage to hold any Georgia real estate license
choice_d: A franchised brokerage's clients are automatically clients of the national franchisor rather than the local firm
explanation: A real estate franchise relationship typically leaves the local brokerage independently owned and operated, licensed and liable in its own right, while paying the franchisor for the right to use its brand, systems, referral network, and marketing -- a structure generally governed by franchise-disclosure requirements informing the franchisee of the material terms of the arrangement before signing.
source_note: hedge: standard national franchise-law doctrine, not Georgia-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is the general purpose of Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act, as distinct from the real estate-specific unfair trade practices enumerated in O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b)?
choice_a: The Fair Business Practices Act applies only to real estate licensees and duplicates § 43-40-25(b) exactly
choice_b: The Fair Business Practices Act has been fully repealed and replaced by O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25
choice_c: The Fair Business Practices Act is a broader Georgia consumer-protection statute prohibiting unfair or deceptive acts or practices in consumer transactions generally, existing alongside (not instead of) the real-estate-specific unfair trade practices GREC enforces against licensees
choice_d: The Fair Business Practices Act applies only to businesses with more than 500 employees
explanation: Georgia's Fair Business Practices Act is a general consumer-protection statute addressing unfair or deceptive acts or practices across consumer transactions broadly, operating alongside (rather than replacing) the real-estate-specific unfair trade practices enumerated in O.C.G.A. § 43-40-25(b) that GREC specifically enforces against licensees.
source_note: hedge: standard content on Georgia's general consumer-protection framework, contrasted with the real-estate-specific statute already covered elsewhere in this bank

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: What is a FinCEN Geographic Targeting Order (GTO), as it has applied to certain U.S. residential real estate transactions?
choice_a: A local zoning designation restricting new residential construction in a specific neighborhood
choice_b: A federal program that provides down-payment assistance grants to first-time homebuyers in targeted areas
choice_c: A type of property tax abatement offered in designated redevelopment zones
choice_d: A federal requirement that title insurance companies in specified areas identify and report the natural persons behind legal entities that pay 'all cash' for high-value residential real estate, as an anti-money-laundering measure
explanation: FinCEN (the U.S. Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) has used Geographic Targeting Orders requiring title insurance companies in specified metropolitan areas to identify and report the beneficial owners behind legal entities making high-value, all-cash residential real estate purchases -- an anti-money-laundering tool aimed at reducing the use of shell companies and cash purchases to launder illicit funds through real estate.
source_note: hedge: standard national content -- federal anti-money-laundering measures affecting real estate closings, not Georgia-statute-specific

topic: General Business Law, Entity Structure, Licensing & Ethics
question: As a matter of general business-entity law, what is the general purpose of registering a trade name (a 'doing business as,' or DBA, name) that differs from a company's legal entity name?
choice_a: It publicly discloses that a business is operating under a name other than its formal legal entity name, so the public and government agencies can identify the actual legal entity responsible for that business, without itself creating a new legal entity
choice_b: A trade name registration creates an entirely new, separate legal entity distinct from the underlying business
choice_c: Trade name registration is required only for businesses with no physical office location
choice_d: A registered trade name automatically transfers all liability from the underlying entity to the trade name itself
explanation: Registering a trade name (DBA) publicly links a business name being used in the marketplace back to the actual underlying legal entity responsible for it, for transparency and accountability purposes -- it does not itself create a new, separate legal entity or alter the underlying entity's liability.
source_note: hedge: standard national business-entity-law content, not Georgia-statute-specific
